idiom_name: lawful getter/setter pair plus a composition operator
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: model a focus as a pair of pure functions - view : Whole -> Focus, and set : (Whole, Focus) -> Whole' where Whole' differs from Whole only in the focus - package the pair as a value, and provide composition (Lens[S,A] and Lens[A,B] give Lens[S,B]). Keep the three laws as the contract: viewing after setting returns the value just set, setting the value that was just viewed is the identity, and of two sets the last wins. Implement the setter with the host language's copy-with primitive so the copy chain lives inside the lens instead of at every call site, and drop to the weaker optics (Optional, Traversal, Prism) when the focus may be absent, repeated or variant-dependent.
code_sketch:
focus = lens(view, set)
  view : Whole -> Focus
  set  : (Whole, Focus) -> Whole'      # only the focus differs
compose(outer, inner) -> lens
  view = w -> inner.view(outer.view(w))
  set  = (w, v) -> outer.set(w, inner.set(outer.view(w), v))
# laws: view(set(w, v)) == v
#       set(w, view(w)) == w
#       last of two sets wins
pitfalls: Writing the setter as an in-place mutation on a shared value: the copy contract is exactly what makes old versions safe to keep and the lens safe to compose.
Encoding a path that may be absent or repeated (optional field, list element) as a total lens instead of the weaker Optional/Traversal.
Skipping the laws and then composing: a setter that normalises or drops unrelated structure produces updates that disagree with direct reads, and nothing flags it.

The 'optics zoo' problem: using Lens where Prism or Traversal is correct (or vice versa) produces confusing APIs and partial setters; learn the taxonomy (Iso → Lens → Affine → Prism → Traversal) before choosing.

Van Laarhoven vs profunctor encoding confusion: Van Laarhoven lenses are prettier but require significant language support (higher-kinded types); profunctor lenses are more portable but have a steeper API. Mixing the two styles in one codebase causes friction.

Runtime overhead in hot paths: each lens composition adds a layer of indirection and closure allocation; in a tight loop updating millions of records, profile before committing to optics over a hand-written copy chain.
Optics library API churn: the optics ecosystem has many competing libraries with incompatible APIs. Choosing a library with a small user base risks maintenance abandonment.

Leaking optics in public API boundaries: exposing Lens[S, A] in a public interface pins the caller to a specific optics library and encoding; prefer returning the updated value or an opaque setter function.

Wrong move: migrate a large Haskell codebase from lens to optics only to shrink dependencies -> that fails when transitive libraries such as swagger2, amazonka, gogol or Chart still expose lens interfaces -> instead inventory the dependency graph and migrate incrementally, keeping qualified adapters at integration boundaries.

Wrong move: use a total Lens for an optional, repeated or variant target -> that fails because a missing or multi-focus target has no single lawful replacement -> instead compose Optional/AffineTraversal, Prism or Traversal and make absence and cardinality explicit.

Wrong move: hand-write a deep setter that also normalises or changes unrelated fields -> that fails getReplace and replaceGet, so composed updates diverge from direct reads -> instead derive the optic or property-test a pure setter against the lens laws.
